extracted.intended_audience: literary students, scholars, and aspiring poets/playwrights interested in Coleridge and poetic/dramatic craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for poetry and poetic drama (suitability for the stage, poetic diction, reception, and professional conduct) as presented in a literary-biographical/critical account of Coleridge's works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding 'metaphysics' in theatre / Readily apprehensible language for the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'metaphysics' is used to denote "whatever is too fine-spun, in the texture of thought and speech, for common wear; whatever is not readily apprehensible and generally acceptable." Mr. Kinnaird may have judged the play to be "too metaphysical for our theatres in their present state."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic works intended for the contemporary public should avoid excessively subtle or fine-spun thought/speech that the general audience cannot readily apprehend; material judged 'metaphysical' may work as a dramatic poem in print but fail as stage fare. (Example: Zapolya was called 'metaphysical' and thus judged unfit for the stage, though it had a favorable audience as a dramatic poem.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction must be required by and in harmony with thought
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mr. C. maintains that Spenser's language is distinct from that of prose, such language being required by his thoughts and in harmony with them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevated or non-prose diction is legitimate when it is demanded by the poet's subject-matter and is in harmony with the thought; poetic diction should arise from and suit the thought rather than be applied gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-poetry warning: ornate diction cannot mask weak thought
rubrics_metrics.description: "Homely thoughts clothed in a glittering tissue of poetic diction are but pseudo-poetry; and the powder on the auricula would be nothing, if the coat itself were not of velvet."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of dressing commonplace or weak ideas in flashy language; ornament without substantive thought constitutes 'pseudo-poetry'. The passage compares styles (Pope/Gray versus Shakespeare/Milton) to illustrate that surface elegance must rest on genuine poetic substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic dramas may not be fully appreciated on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: "This drama is a strain of poetry, and like all, not only dramatic poems, but highly poetic dramas, not to be fully appreciated on the stage."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly poetic dramatic works can be artistically valuable but may fail to translate into theatrical success; assess genre suitability (poem vs. performance) when writing or staging such works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional expectation: patience and tempered hopes for reward
rubrics_metrics.description: "My Father's whole history is a lesson to the professors of literature, and that which relates to the Remorse is a small but significant part of it, teaching patience and hope, while it may serve to repress the expectation, that money and credit can soon and certainly be obtained..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspiring writers should cultivate patience and hope; do not assume that genius or introductions guarantee quick financial reward or credit. The anecdote of a delayed/initially-rejected play illustrates the professional reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception and success measured by sales, audience, and receipts
rubrics_metrics.description: Success is reported by concrete reception metrics: e.g., "2000 copies were sold in six weeks," a play was performed "with unbounded applause thirty successive nights," and an author could expect "8,000l. or 10,000l." from theatrical success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popularity, sales figures, audience applause, and financial returns are used as pragmatic indicators of success; however, these measures may not align perfectly with artistic judgment or long-term critical estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial/textual accuracy matters (punctuation and printing)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An important error in punctuation has crept into the later editions of Zapolya... the note of admiration is placed after 'visitations' at the end of line 23; whereas it should be placed at the end of line 2."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention to correct punctuation and faithful textual editing is necessary for quality editions; mispunctuation can alter meaning or disrupt the intended reading and should be corrected in later prints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should represent arguments fairly
rubrics_metrics.description: The author objects to misrepresentation: "To say that he decided 'the contrary', as if he had denied poetic diction to Spenser, is not like the auricula's coat, candid."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical readers and reviewers should avoid misrepresenting an author's positions; fair, accurate representation of arguments and contexts is a standard of good criticism.
